newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - U.S. states settle with Liggett on tobacco.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - U.S. states settle with Liggett on tobacco.

text.p: By Gail Appleson, Law Corresponden

In the harshest blow yet to the cigarette industry, Liggett Group agreed on Thursday to settle tobacco litigation with almost half of the nation's attorneys general and give up potentially devastating documents.

The historic accord calls for unprecedented concessions from Liggett, owned by Bennett LeBow's Brooke Group Ltd., that also include the company's agreement to allow current and former employees -- including its lawyers -- to testify against the rest of the industry.
The accord was reached with all 22 attorneys general who have sued the industry to recoup Medicaid health care costs of smoking.

Another key part of the settlement provides that Liggett become the first tobacco company to admit the health hazards of smoking and that it is addictive. It has agreed to include labels on its cigarettes warning about the hazards of nicotine.

"I believe this is the beginning of the end for this conspiracy of lies and deception that has been perpetrated on the American public by the tobacco companies. Somebody is finally telling the truth," Arizona Attorney General Grant Woods told a news conference.
He also emphasized that the company admits that tobacco companies actively market to teenagers.
"Liggett says publicly and for first time that for any tobacco executive for any tobacco company, for any person to say contrary, is a lie. They know it and they will help us prove it," Woods said.

The settlement could prove damaging to the other tobacco companies on many fronts. Among the most devastating effects is that the documents might be used by the Justice Department, which is investigating the industry for criminal wrongdoing.
Its probe includes whether top tobacco executives lied to congress when they testified in 1994 that nicotine is not addictive.
The attorneys general said they might also use the documents to bring criminal cases in their individual states.

Mississippi Attorney Michael Moore, who has spearheaded the litigation, said the agreement by Liggett to turn over evidence and allow employees and counsel to testify will bring the industry "to its knees."
"They (Liggett employees) are going to have to appear in every one of our cases...Think of this, their lawyers are going to be on our team fighting the other side," he said.
"Never again will Big Tobacco be able to claim innocence with a straight face." Moore said.
The Mississippi case is scheduled to be the first Medicaid case to go to trial on June 2.
The settlement also includes what could prove to be a small monetary settlement in which Liggett will pay states 25 percent of its pre-tax profits for the next 25 years to settle claims.
The attorneys general emphasized that the pact was not reached for money.
"Our goal was to change the way this industry does business...it will have to get out of the lives of our children," Woods said.
States that have not sued the industry have six months to decide whether to participate in the settlement.
Minnesota Attorney General Hubert Humphrey said the same deal will not be offered to other tobacco companies.

"I think we need to put this in perspective -- this is a little bit like busting a street drug dealer to get at the Colombia drug cartel. .... this is a one-time deal... The terms offered to Liggett today to come clean are not going to be offered to others. We're very serious about going ahead and making sure that the entire industry is transformed...," he said.

Earlier Thursday, the larger tobacco companies got a restraining order from a North Carolina state court preventing Liggett from turning over documents that are protected by attorney client privilege.
The attorneys general said they were not worried about the order because it is not binding in other states and because if the documents provide evidence of crime they would not be privileged.
In addition, the documents are being turned over to judges presiding over the state cases who will determine if they can be used as evidence.
Liggett has been asked by the states to isolate the 25 most damaging documents. The attorneys general said the documents were being sent to courthouses Thursday.
"They will be all over the country by the time the sun comes up," Woods said.
